transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I... I suppose I'm here because things have just gotten too heavy. My sister actually drove me, but I came in because I just keep thinking, every single night when I finally lay down, that it would just be so much better if I didn't wake up. Like, if the morning just didn't happen for me and I could just slip away in my sleep. It wouldn't just be easier, it would be right. 

I do flooring for a living—tile, carpet, a lot of hard labor on your knees all day, you know? I work with a really good crew. Or, I used to. But lately, I just... I feel like dying would be the fair punishment for what I've done to my family and my crew. I've just completely ruined everything for them, brought all this down on them, and I can't fix it. I can't go to the job sites, I can't face the guys, I can't look my family in the eye. I can't do anything but lay there and think about how my being dead is the only way to make it right. It's just this constant, heavy loop in my head that I deserve to be punished, that not waking up is the only fair price for the damage I've caused everyone who relies on me. So I just lay there, hoping my heart just stops so they can finally be free of me.
How long have you been having these thoughts about not waking up and feeling like you deserve to be punished?

Well, it's... it's been a long time. It feels like forever, honestly, but if I really think about it, sit down and trace it back... it's been about a year and two months. Yeah, a year and two months of this... this crushing weight. It started a few months after my husband's injury. He got hurt, and at first, I was just running on adrenaline, you know? Just trying to keep the house afloat, keep the bills paid, keep working my jobs. I was doing tile in this huge commercial building downtown, working ten, sometimes twelve-hour days, coming home, taking care of him, doing everything. 

But then, a few months after it happened, when things were supposed to be settling into a routine, that's when it just... it fell on me. The darkness, I mean. It just settled over me like a thick, heavy blanket and it hasn't lifted since. A year and two months of waking up—when I do manage to sleep—and just immediately feeling that dread, that absolute certainty that I am the problem. I can remember the exact week it started getting really bad, too. It was right around the time the leaves started changing last year, and I remember looking out the window of the truck on the way to a job site and thinking, 'I shouldn't be here. I don't deserve to be here.' And it's just been every single day since then. Fourteen months of just... waiting for the end, because the guilt is just so loud.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before these thoughts started?

No, no, I really don't. It's funny you ask that, because I used to be such a... I don't know, a vibrant person? I used to do so much. Before my husband got hurt, before all this guilt just started eating me alive, I had a whole life outside of the flooring jobs. I used to paint, for one. Watercolors, mostly. I'd set up my easel in the sunroom on Sunday mornings and just get lost in the colors for hours. I loved mixing them, watching how they bled into the paper. And cooking—oh, I used to cook these huge, elaborate meals for the two of us, or even invite the crew over for a big barbecue on the weekends. I'd spend all day prepping, marinating, baking from scratch. It was my way of showing love, I guess.

And I used to be so active, too. I'd go for a three-mile run every single morning before I even strapped on my knee pads for work. It cleared my head, got me ready for the day. I even did community theater! I know, a tile installer doing theater, it sounds silly, but I loved it. I never missed a rehearsal, I knew all my lines, I loved the energy of being on stage. 

But now... now it's all just gone. The easel has been folded up in the closet for over a year. The paint tubes are probably dried out. If I even think about cooking, it just feels like this insurmountable mountain of effort. We eat frozen dinners, or my sister brings food, because the thought of chopping an onion just... it drains whatever tiny bit of energy I have left. I haven't run a single step, and the theater group actually called me a few times when I stopped showing up, but I just ignored the calls. I just didn't care. I still don't care. All those things... painting, cooking, running, the plays... they feel like they belong to somebody else entirely. Like chores from a life I don't even recognize anymore. I just can't bring myself to care if I miss out on them, because honestly, I don't think I deserve to enjoy them anyway. I just sit there and think about how I shouldn't be allowed to have fun when everything is so broken.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than you used to, or that it takes you longer to do things?

Well, I... I don't know if I'm moving slower, exactly. I mean, maybe? I haven't really paid attention to how long it takes me to do things because I'm just not doing much of anything at all. Like I said, I'm not going to the job sites, I'm not running, I'm not cooking. I just lay there. So I don't really have a good way to measure if I'm moving slower than I used to. 

I guess when I do have to get up, like to go to the bathroom or if my sister forces me to come sit in the living room while she's here, it feels like... like walking through water, maybe? But I don't know if that's because my body is actually moving slower or if it's just that the weight of everything is so heavy that it feels like it takes a massive amount of effort just to put one foot in front of the other. It's like my limbs are filled with lead, you know? But as for actually timing myself or noticing if it takes me twenty minutes to do something that used to take five... I really couldn't tell you. I'm just so stuck in my own head, in that loop of knowing I've ruined everything, that I don't really notice what my physical body is doing most of the time. I'm just... existing, barely. So, I don't know. I'm not sure.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past year?

Well, yeah, I have... I've definitely lost weight. It's not like I'm trying to, though. I mean, who tries to lose weight when everything else is falling apart? But my clothes... my work pants, especially. I have these heavy-duty canvas pants that I used to wear to the job sites, you know, with the reinforced knees for all the tile work. I put them on the other day—just to see if I could even still fit into my old life, I guess—and they were just hanging off me. I had to pull my belt in three notches past where it used to sit, and even then, they looked baggy. It's like I'm just shrinking away.

And it's because I just... I don't eat. I forget. Or, it's not even that I forget, it's that the thought of food just doesn't even register most of the time. I'll wake up—if you can call it waking up—and the whole day will just blur past me. The sun goes down, and I'll realize I haven't had a single thing since the day before. And when my sister comes over and forces me to eat, or if I finally realize my stomach is cramping and I try to force down some toast or a few bites of whatever she brought... I just feel sick. Like, physically nauseous. I'll take two bites and my throat just closes up. It feels like my body is rejecting it, like I don't even deserve the nourishment, you know? Like I'm being punished from the inside out. So yeah, the weight is just falling off because I can't bring myself to eat more than a few bites before I feel like I'm going to throw up. It's just... it's just another thing that's fading away.
Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people couldn't hear or see?

I... well, yes. I didn't want to tell anyone about this because I know how it sounds, but yes, I have. It's actually really terrifying, to be honest with you. It started happening a while ago, and it's always this... this man's voice. 

I'll be in my kitchen, right? And my kitchen is this tight little galley style, so it's narrow, with the fridge at one end by the back door and the sink right under this little window that looks out into the side yard. I'll just be standing there, maybe staring out the window, not even doing anything, just frozen and stuck in my head like I usually am these days. And suddenly, right behind my shoulder—usually my left shoulder—I'll hear him. 

It's not a whisper, and it's not like a thought in my head, if that makes sense. It's loud and clear, exactly as if a real, physical person has snuck up right behind me and is standing inches away. He says things like, "You missed it." Or he'll say, "Everyone knows." And the tone... it's so deep and cold and accusatory. It sends this horrible chill right down my spine, all the way to my tailbone. I whip around, my heart just pounding out of my chest, fully expecting to see a man standing right there on the linoleum, but the kitchen is completely empty. The back door is locked and deadbolted. There is absolutely no one there. 

And it's not just at home, either. It used to happen at the job sites, back when I was still trying to force myself to work. I remember this one specific time, I was laying this ceramic subway tile in a client's master bathroom. It was this huge, echoing room with these awful vaulted ceilings, and I was on my knees, troweling the thinset onto the wall, just trying to focus. And then I heard it. Same voice. Right behind me. "Everyone knows." I dropped my trowel and spun around so fast I nearly knocked over my whole bucket of mortar. I was ready to yell at whoever had sneaked up on me. But it was just me. Just me and the tile. The homeowner wasn't even home, the house was completely empty. 

But I heard him. I swear to you, doctor, I heard him as clearly as I hear you speaking to me right now. It's driving me out of my mind because I know nobody is there when I turn around, but the voice is so incredibly real. How can it be so real if the room is empty? It just... it feeds right into that horrible guilt I was telling you about. It's like this invisible person is just following me around, confirming every single awful thing I already feel about myself, and I can't make him stop.
How often do you hear the man's voice?

Well, it's... I mean, it's happening almost every day now. Sometimes multiple times a day. It’s not just a rare, one-off thing, which is why it’s so incredibly exhausting. I’ll wake up, and for a split second, I might forget, but then I'm just waiting for it, my whole body just tense. 

Like I was just telling you about being in the kitchen or back when I was at the job sites... it happens so often that I'm constantly on edge, just waiting for that man's voice to come from right behind my shoulder. And it doesn't matter how many times it happens in a week, it always catches me completely off guard. I'll hear him say, "You missed it," or "Everyone knows," and it is so loud and so clear, exactly as if someone is standing right there, sharing my breathing space. 

And every single time—every time, doctor, whether it's twice a day or four times a day—I turn around expecting to see him. I whip around because my brain tells me, "There is a physical human being standing inches behind you." And then... nobody's there. Just the empty kitchen, or the empty room. And then I'll just sit there for hours, completely paralyzed, analyzing it and wondering when he's going to say it again. I'll just be waiting for the next time. So, yeah, it's frequent. It's just this relentless, everyday thing now, and I can't escape it.
Do you find it difficult to express your thoughts or to keep track of what you're saying when we're talking?

Yeah... I mean, yes, I do. It's actually really frustrating because in my head, everything makes perfect sense, but when it comes out of my mouth, people just look at me like I'm speaking a different language. 

Like, for example, back when I was still trying to work, if someone—maybe my sister or a client—asked me to explain what happened on a job, or why a project was taking so long. I'll start trying to explain it to them, right? And I'll start talking about the tile lines, because you have to get the grout lines perfectly straight, especially if you're working with those large-format porcelain tiles, otherwise the whole room just looks entirely crooked and the eye goes right to the mistake. But then, just thinking about lifting those heavy tiles makes my brain jump straight to my husband's back brace. You know, the heavy black one with the rigid metal stays in the back that he had to wear after he threw his back out unloading the work truck that one time, and how the velcro on it was always getting full of lint and wearing out. 

And then, just from thinking about that brace, my mind automatically jumps over to the license paperwork. Because I remember we had to file the contractor license renewal and all the liability insurance forms right around the exact same time he hurt his back, and the city was being so incredibly difficult about the permits for that specific job... 

And before I know it, I'm talking about the permit office downtown and the lady behind the glass, and whoever I'm talking to will just stop me. They'll hold up their hands and tell me I'm not answering the question. They'll say, "What does any of this have to do with the bathroom floor?" And it just makes me feel so... broken, I guess. Because to me, it's a perfectly straight line. The tile lines, the back brace, the paperwork... it all feels completely connected in my head. It's all part of the exact same story, the exact same memory, and I don't understand how they don't see how it all links together. But I guess to everyone else, my thoughts are just jumping all over the place and making no sense at all. So, yeah, it is really hard to keep track, because I feel like I'm giving all the necessary details to paint the whole picture, but nobody else can follow the thread.
Do you often find yourself having trouble sticking to one topic when talking to others?

Well, yeah, that's exactly what I was just trying to explain to you with the whole... the whole thing about the bathroom tile and my husband's back brace. That's exactly it. 

It's like... people think I'm going off-topic, right? They think I'm just wandering away from the point or that I can't focus. If someone asks me a simple question, they expect this simple, straight-line answer. But in my head, it doesn't work like that. The topic isn't just one tiny little box. When I try to explain what happened on a job, I can't just say "it took longer than expected." I have to explain the tile lines, because the tile lines are the foundation, and that heavy lifting directly connects to the back brace, which directly connects to the license paperwork we were filing at the exact same time. 

So when you ask if I have trouble sticking to one topic... to me, I *am* sticking to the topic! It is all one topic. It’s all one big, connected web in my brain. But my sister, or whoever I'm talking to, they'll just cut me off right in the middle of me explaining it. They'll hold up their hands and just sigh and say, "Can you please just stick to the point?" And I'm sitting there, just completely deflated, thinking, I *am* sticking to the point! How do you not see that the back brace and the permit office are the exact reason the job went the way it did? 

It’s so incredibly exhausting trying to talk to anyone these days. I feel like I have to explain every single detail so they can understand the full picture of what I'm saying, but they just lose patience with me. They just tell me I'm not answering the question, even though I'm giving them all the answers, all the context they could possibly need. It makes me want to just stop talking to people altogether, to be honest with you, because what is the point of even opening my mouth if nobody is willing to follow along with how everything is connected?
Have you experienced periods of time where you felt extremely low in mood, but then returned to a normal mood?

Well, yeah, I guess there was a time like that... I mean, it’s not like it ever fully goes away, but there was a stretch, maybe a couple of months ago, where things felt a little lighter, just for a bit. It lasted for several weeks, actually. I remember because I actually started getting out of bed before noon, which was huge for me. I was making myself breakfast again—just toast and tea, usually, but still, I was eating a little better instead of just staring at the wall all day. And the crying stopped. I wasn't just sitting on the edge of the bed sobbing for hours on end like I had been for months prior. I actually felt like I had a little bit of energy, like maybe I was returning to some version of normal, you know?

But the thing is, doctor, even when my mood lifted, even when I wasn't feeling so incredibly heavy and hopeless... the other stuff didn't stop. It never stopped. I was still hearing that man’s voice every single day. I'd be at work, trying to measure out a room for carpet, feeling okay mood-wise, and then—bam—he’d be right over my shoulder telling me I missed it. And I was still absolutely convinced, without a shadow of a doubt, that the clients and the suppliers were tracking me. I knew they were keeping tabs on my every move, watching where I bought my materials, monitoring how long I stayed at a job site. So, yes, my mood got better for a few weeks, I felt almost normal in that regard, but the voice and the... the knowing that I was being watched... that never took a break. It just kept right on going, even when I wasn't crying.
Have you ever experienced a period where you felt extremely high in mood or energy?

High in mood? Like... really energetic? No. No, never. I mean, I honestly don't even know what that would feel like, to be honest with you. 

Even on my absolute best days, even years ago before everything got so incredibly heavy and complicated... I was never one of those people who just bounces off the walls or feels on top of the world. You have to understand, my line of work—installing carpet, laying down tile, hauling boxes of porcelain and those massive, heavy rolls of carpet padding up and down flights of stairs all day—it just drains every single ounce of energy out of you. It is completely physical, back-breaking work. You come home and your knees are throbbing, your hands are completely raw and calloused from using the carpet kicker, and the dust is just settled deep into your skin. So the idea of having "extreme energy" or feeling "extremely high" in mood... it just doesn't even compute for me. 

Even during that brief window I was just telling you about, when I felt a little lighter and started making myself toast in the mornings again? That wasn't a high. That wasn't extra energy. That was just... baseline. That was just me finally scraping together barely enough energy to exist like a normal human being for a few hours. I have never felt elated, or like I could take on the world, or like my mind was racing with all these amazing, happy ideas. It's always just been this constant, exhausting push to get through the day, to get the room measurements right, to deal with the suppliers and the clients without collapsing. 

So, no. I've never had a period like that. I honestly wish I did have a little extra energy sometimes, just to get through the day-to-day things like the laundry or the billing paperwork, but no... never anything extreme or high like you're talking about. Just tired. Always just tired.
Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely high in mood or irritable, and also had increased energy or activity?

No, like I was just saying... I haven't ever felt anything like that. Irritable, sure, sometimes, because when you're on your hands and knees all day and someone is asking you a million questions about grout color, you get a little snappy. But not... not like what you're saying, with the extreme mood or the high energy. 

I mean, I don't think people realize just how much physical toll this job takes. You don't just bounce back from carrying a hundred-pound roll of Berber up three flights of stairs. You don't get a sudden burst of energy to go do things. You just want to sit in a chair and not move for twelve hours. So the idea of being highly active or having all this extra energy... it's just not something that happens in my life. It's just not. Even before everything got so bad, before the crying and the voice and all of it... I was just a normal, tired person doing a hard job. I've never had a time where I felt like I was buzzing or anything like that.
Have you ever had a period where the voice you're hearing or the feelings of being watched were not present when you were feeling your lowest or most anxious?

Well, no... no, actually, they were always there. Especially then. I mean, when I was at my absolute worst, when things were just incredibly dark and heavy... the voice and the watching, they didn't go away. If anything, it all just kind of tangled together. 

I remember this one stretch, it was months long, where I was just so low. I was barely eating anything, maybe just picking at some saltines if I even remembered. I was losing weight, and I just had this constant, overwhelming feeling of guilt, like everything that was wrong in the world was somehow my fault. I'd lay in bed for hours, just staring at the ceiling, and honestly, doctor, I was really just wishing I wouldn't wake up the next morning. I didn't want to do it anymore. The exhaustion was just so deep in my bones, not just from the carpet installing, but just from existing. 

And during all of that, during those awful, awful months... the man's voice was right there with me. He didn't take a break just because I was miserable. He'd be right there, commenting on how useless I was, telling me I was messing up even when I was just lying there doing nothing. And the paranoia—the absolute certainty that I was being watched—that was happening at the exact same time. Every time my phone rang for a job, I just knew, I knew in my gut, that it wasn't a real client. It was a setup. They were calling to try and catch me in a mistake, to expose me for whatever it was they thought I was doing wrong. Even the patterns on the floor... I'd look down at the tile I was supposed to be laying, and I could see how the lines and the shapes were deliberately designed to trap me, to reveal something about me. 

So, no, they never stopped. Even when I was feeling my absolute lowest, when I was so depressed I could barely breathe... the voice and the feeling of being exposed, they were right there alongside it. It's like they were all happening at once, this huge, overwhelming mess of just feeling terrible and terrified at the same time.
Do you believe that the voice you're hearing or the feelings of being watched are real?

Well... yes. I mean, of course they're real. You ask if I believe they're real, but it's not really a matter of belief, doctor, it's just... it's what is actually happening. It's my life. Because even on the days when the heaviness lifts a tiny bit, you know? Even on the days when I'm actually up and out of the house, when I'm not crying or just down in bed wishing the day would end... I still know exactly what they're doing. I see it as clear as day. 

The homeowners, the suppliers I buy the mortar and the grout from... they are all in on it. They are using everything they can to track me. Like, the floor patterns. I mentioned the lines and shapes earlier, but it goes so much deeper than that. They specifically choose these intricate herringbone or chevron patterns, or they request these really specific, complicated tile layouts, not because it looks good in their kitchen, but because it's a test. They use the patterns to track whether I'm ruining the jobs on purpose. 

And it's not just the floors, either. It's the texts I get from the suppliers about backordered materials, or the random calls I get from the city about building permits—it's all coordinated. They send those texts and make those permit calls at very specific times to keep tabs on me, to see if I'm slipping up, to build this whole elaborate case that I'm intentionally destroying their properties and messing up the installations. 

People try to tell me I'm crazy for thinking this. My sister will say, "Oh, you're just stressed, it's just a normal permit check, the supplier is just running late because of the supply chain." But they don't see it. They don't see the coordination. No one can talk me out of it because I am the one living it. I am the one putting my hands on that tile and seeing the trap they've laid out. I get absolutely certain about it, because the proof is right there in the texts and the floor layouts. So yes, it is absolutely real. I know for a fact they are tracking me to prove I'm ruining these jobs, and nothing anybody says is going to change what I can see right in front of my own two eyes.
Do you believe the people tracking you are actually out to harm you?

Well, harm me... I don't know if "harm" is the right word. I mean, not like they're going to come up behind me with a pipe while I'm cutting baseboards, you know? It's not... it's not physical violence, I don't think. At least, I haven't seen any evidence of that yet. But they want to ruin me. They want to destroy my livelihood and my reputation. 

I've thought about this a lot, doctor, lying awake at night, just turning it over and over in my head. Why me? Why go through all this trouble with the floor patterns and the supplier texts? And it's because they want to catch me in a lie. They want to prove that I'm incompetent, that I'm a fraud, that I'm doing a terrible job on purpose. They want to strip away everything I've worked for. I've been doing this for over fifteen years. I started as an apprentice right after I dropped out of college, carrying buckets of thinset that weighed more than I did, ruining my knees before I was even thirty. I built a reputation as someone who does clean, precise work. And now... now they want to take all of that and twist it.

So, are they out to harm me? Yes, in a way that matters more than just a punch in the face. They want to expose me, humiliate me, and probably make sure I never work again. And the voice... the man's voice, he agrees. He tells me they're right to do it, that I deserve to be exposed because I'm a failure anyway. So it's not just that they're tracking me, it's that they're building a case. A massive, undeniable case against me. And honestly, the anticipation of when they're finally going to drop the hammer and take everything away... it's exhausting. It's just so exhausting.
Do you believe the voice you're hearing is trying to communicate a specific message to you or is it just random?

Well, it's definitely not random. Not at all. It feels incredibly specific, like it's aimed right at the core of me. It’s a man’s voice, and he’s not just babbling nonsense or making background noise. He has these very specific things he says, and they always tie right into whatever I'm doing or whatever I'm terrified of in that moment. 

For instance, I'll be at a job site, right? I'll be down on my hands and knees, maybe smoothing out the adhesive or trying to get the grout lines perfectly straight—because, like I was saying before, if they aren't straight, I know they'll use it against me. So I'm down there, hyper-focused, and right behind me, just right over my shoulder, I'll hear him say, "You missed it." Just like that. Or I'll be at home, off the clock, just standing in my own kitchen trying to make a cup of coffee or staring at the sink, and the voice will come from right behind me and say, "Everyone knows." 

And I mean, doctor, it is so incredibly clear. It's not like a thought echoing in my head, or like a memory, or the wind, or the pipes settling in the house. It sounds exactly like a physical, living, breathing human being is standing inches away from the back of my neck. It’s so real and so loud that every single time it happens, my heart just jumps right up into my throat and I whip around. I'll drop my trowel on the floor, or I'll spill my coffee on the counter, and I spin around fully expecting to see a man standing right there in my kitchen or on the job site. I brace myself for it. 

But... when I turn around, nobody's there. It's just empty space. Just the cabinets, or the unfinished drywall. But the message itself? Yes, the message is very clear and very specific. He wants me to know that I'm failing, that I've missed something important, and that everyone is completely aware of what a fraud I am. It's this deliberate, targeted commentary, and it just never really stops.
Do you think the people who you believe are tracking you are trying to hurt you physically or just damage your reputation?

I mean... I think I just went over this, doctor. Like I was just explaining a minute ago, it's not a physical thing. They aren't trying to beat me up or, you know, push me down a flight of stairs at a job site or something. Why would they even need to? My body is already completely wrecked from this job anyway. If you spend fifteen years on your knees scraping up old linoleum and laying down heavy ceramic tile, your back and your joints are already destroyed, so physical pain isn't really the ultimate threat here. 

No, it's... it's exactly what I was just saying, it's my reputation. It's my entire livelihood. In the flooring business, especially around here where all the general contractors talk to each other at the supply houses... reputation is literally everything. If word gets around that you're sloppy, or worse, that you're intentionally sabotaging a layout—like if you mess up the grout lines on a custom master bathroom floor that some homeowner just paid ten thousand dollars for in materials alone—you are completely done. You will never get another bid. 

And that is exactly what they want. They want to completely dismantle my name. They want to make it so that when someone asks a supplier about me, all they hear is that I'm a complete fraud who ruins properties. It's so much worse than physical harm, because physical harm heals, you know? A broken arm heals, a cut heals. But if they convince the whole city that I'm incompetent and malicious, I lose everything I've spent my entire adult life building since I left college. And honestly, with how incredibly heavy and dark everything feels lately, with me barely able to even drag myself out from under the covers most mornings... I don't have the energy to fight them on it. I just don't. They know I'm weak right now, they know I'm struggling just to exist, and they're using that exact timing to destroy my name. So yeah, like I said, it's not my body they're after. It's my whole life.
Do you believe the voice you're hearing and the feelings of being watched are part of a plot against you?

Well, "plot" makes it sound like some kind of spy movie, but... yes. Absolutely yes. It’s all connected. And the thing is, doctor, this isn't just some passing thought I have when I'm feeling really low. I know I've talked about how heavy everything gets, how I spend days just completely paralyzed by it. But even when that lifts a little? Even when I'm not crying or down in bed, and I actually have the energy to stand up and go to a site, this... this reality doesn't change. I get absolutely certain—I mean, I *am* certain—that the homeowners and the suppliers are all in on it together. 

They have this whole elaborate system to track me, to monitor every single move I make to see whether I'm ruining their jobs on purpose. And they use the most mundane things to do it, which is how they think they're getting away with it. They use the floor patterns, for one. Like, I'll be mapping out a complex herringbone layout, or even just a standard one-third offset for wood-look plank tile, and I can see how the boxes were left in the room by the delivery guys, or how the chalk lines on the subfloor were marked before I even got there. It’s a grid. It's a way of boxing me in and watching me. 

And then there are the texts from the suppliers. You'd think a text saying my mortar is ready for pickup or that a certain grout color is on backorder is just a normal message, right? But it's not. The timing of it, the specific wording they use... it coordinates perfectly with exactly what I'm doing in that exact moment. And the permit calls! The homeowners will stand out in the hallway and pretend they're just calling the city to check on the inspection schedules or the plumbing permits, but I know they're actually calling to log my hours, to report back on whether I'm intentionally sabotaging their bathrooms or messing up the transitions. 

People try to tell me I'm overthinking it. People who don't work in the trades, they try to tell me that a text from a supplier is just a text, or that the homeowner is just anxious about their remodel. But no one can talk me out of it. They can talk until they're blue in the face, but I know what I'm seeing. I know what's happening. I've been doing this too long to miss the signs. They are meticulously tracking whether I'm ruining these jobs on purpose, and that voice I hear? He’s just the narrator for the whole sick operation, making sure I know they're watching.
